note: Twenty-three printables, plus 01b — an A3 alternative to the sound-frame mat, made by the same builder and by the Writing Shelf generator at /montree/library/tools/writing-shelf-generator. All adult-facing text sits outside the cards. CUT ONCE: cards butt against each other with no gutters, and every cut line runs the full width or the full height of the page, edge to edge, so one straight stroke of the blade separates the cards on both sides of it. The lines are light-grey 0.25 mm hairlines — they are cut away, so a line IS the card edge — and a small black triangle at the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin marks each line where it meets the paper edge, because a hairline dies in the last few millimetres of any printer. Card content stops 4 mm inside every card edge, so a wandering blade never touches a photograph or a word. Footer on every sheet: “Cut along every grey line · N cards”. Sheets 02, 03, 06, 13 and 14 are MOUNTED on coloured backing card with a 1 cm border, so their printed size is 20 mm smaller than the finished card; 04, 05, 09, 11, 12 and 17 are not mounted and print at finished size. Sheet 14’s backing card is not any colour: PINK for its tier 1 cards, BLUE for its tier 2 and GREEN for its tier 3, because on that sheet the colour IS the reading level. Sheet 12’s card is no longer a fixed 60 × 35 mm: it is 28 mm tall and MEASURED to its own word’s ink, set in Comic Neue at an x-height of exactly 6.6 mm — sheet 15’s writing rule — so a word he lifts out of the Tray 5 tin is the size of the word he writes under it. Sheet 17 is the one sheet whose pages take different stock: pages 1–2 are plain paper and are worked on, never cut and never laminated, and page 3 alone is 250 gsm card, laminated and cut. Sheets 18 and 19 are the magnetic pair and they cut ACROSS ONLY: a cut guide sits at every row boundary, full width, in the same hairline-and-triangle standard, so a page may be left whole as one tier mat or cut into six row mats — but never down, because a row is one piece, picture and line together. Neither is ever laminated: a laminated magnet will not hold a magnetic card.

items.title: Word-card tins — three tier tins and a free set, 164 cards, 28 mm tall
items.note: FOUR SETS, NOT ONE TIN, and every word printed at the size the child WRITES it. Three SELF-CONTAINED tier tins — pink 62 cards, blue 20, green 37 — each holding every word its own tier's sentences need ACROSS BOTH TRAY 5 DECKS, in the number they need ALL AT ONCE, so a word shared across tiers is simply printed again in each tin and no tin can be half of a sentence. BOTH DECKS, AND THE COUNT IS A SUM (2026-09-14). Two changes, off a morning in the classroom. FIRST, THE TIN COUNTED ONLY SHEET 14: tier_need() read sheet 14's cards and nothing else, so sheet 13's FOURTEEN STORY STARTERS were never in the tin at all — nineteen words (mat, pen, dog, log, bug, rug, rat, hat, nut, hut, pan, cub, bog, bee, tree, duck, truck, sheep, asleep) had no card, and not one starter had the capitalised lead word it opens on, so a child could pick a story starter off the tray and not be able to build it. The tins are now derived from BOTH decks — sheet 13's fourteen (10 pink, 0 blue, 4 green) and sheet 14's eighteen (6 pink, 6 blue, 6 green), thirty-two sentences — and sheet 13's phrases go through build_14.display_words() exactly like sheet 14's, so `cat on a mat` asks the tin for `Cat`, `on`, `a` and `mat.`; sheet 13's own deck still prints lower case, as it always has. SECOND, THE COUNT IS A SUM AND NO LONGER A MAXIMUM: “the most any single sentence needs” builds a tin you can make ONE sentence out of, and the work is laying the whole tier out on the mat together, so pink holds `a` eleven times over because eleven of its sixteen sentences want one. check_buildable() re-derives from sheets 13 and 14 that all thirty-two sentences are SIMULTANEOUSLY buildable out of what the sheet prints, and refuses to build otherwise; `--check` runs it with a negative control. THE TIN HOLDS THE PRINTED FORM, NOT THE LEDGER WORD (2026-09-13). The sentences print as proper sentences now — a capital on the first word, a full stop on the last — and the STOP IS BAKED INTO THE LAST WORD CARD rather than carried by a tile of its own, the owner's explicit choice. So a tin holds `The` and `A` where a sentence opens on them, `sat.` and `wig.` where one closes on them, and BOTH forms where one tier needs both: green carries `The` beside `the` and `sat` beside `sat.`, because “The sad dad sat in the sand.” wants the first of each pair while three of its neighbours end on the second. Many cards of the same word in one tin is correct, not a duplicate to be tidied away. build_14.display_words() is the one transform and this sheet derives the tins from it; nothing here types a capital or a full stop. The fourth set is UNCOLOURED and is for FREE COMPOSITION: the 35 reader words no sentence card on EITHER deck uses, plus 10 blanks, so the tin grows as the readers do. THE CARD IS MEASURED, not fixed: its width is the word's own INK width plus G, the word space — a constant 7.0 mm of clear paper between two butted words — to the nearest 0.1 mm, with exactly G/2 of paper each side of the word, so `a` is a 12.3 mm sliver and `penguin` is 51.2 mm. Butt any two cards and the space from the last ink of one word to the first ink of the next is 7.0 mm, whatever letters meet. SEVEN MILLIMETRES WAS CHOSEN BY EYE, printed at true scale against 4.0, 5.0, 5.909 (the ink width of a lowercase `o`, the derivation it was picked over) and 8.5 mm: it is the gap that reads as a real word space without opening into a hole. It is measured on the glyph OUTLINES and not on the advance box: the advance carries each glyph's side bearings, and padding by it holds the paper constant while the space the eye reads swings from 2.85 to 6.17 mm. One letter of paper is the space a hand actually leaves, and it is the spacing he then copies into his book. The old 60 × 35 mm card gave `a` and `splash` the same width and taught him to leave gigantic uneven gaps. THE X-HEIGHT IS 6.6 mm EXACTLY — the ruled line of sheet 15's writing book — solved from the Comic Neue TTF's own OS/2.sxHeight (38.4161 pt) and verified by rasterising a probe glyph, never guessed, so a word he picks out of the tin and the word he writes under it are the same size. Comic Neue is sheets 13/14/15's face, not sheet 04's Fredoka: the tin is a WRITING material now. THE TIER COLOUR IS THE BASELINE — a 0.5 mm rule running the full width of the card, edge to edge, with the word drawn over it so descenders cross it as they do on ruled paper; butted cards join their rules into ONE continuous coloured line under the whole sentence. The free set's rule is a neutral charcoal, the absence of a tier and not a fourth one. No frame, no tint, no label. THE GRAMMAR SYMBOL IS ON THE FRONT, CENTRED ABOVE THE WORD, and it is TINY — 3.6 mm, against a word whose x-height alone is 6.6 mm. It is not a sorting mark and it is not a label: it sits exactly where the full-size Tray 8 token will be laid when the child comes to that work, so the card is quietly showing him the shape he will one day put there. He can point at it and ask what it is, and he can read the grammar of a sentence he has already built with his own hands. An earlier cut of this sheet put the symbol on the BACK, to make the card its own control of error by flipping; the owner overruled it (2026-09-13) for the reason above, and the sheet is SINGLE-SIDED again. The symbol's TOP sits 2.5 mm down from the card's top edge and check() proves at least 1.5 mm of paper between its foot and the tallest ascender on that card, card by card, refusing to build otherwise. Blank cards carry no symbol. SEVEN PARTS OF SPEECH, NOT THREE LENGTH BUCKETS. The tin used to sort into “naming / doing / small words”, and `small` was not a grammar — it was a bucket for anything short, holding the, a, in, and, it, my, wet and top at once. The symbols are now the standard Montessori ones and the classes are real: black triangle noun (48 words), red circle verb (15), dark blue triangle adjective (12), light blue triangle article (2), green crescent preposition (4), purple triangle pronoun (1), pink bar conjunction (1). The scale is part of the symbol, as it is on the Tray 8 tokens — the article's triangle is smaller than the adjective's, which is smaller than the noun's — and check() refuses to build unless the seven classes cover the ledger EXACTLY: no word unclassified, no classified word missing from the tin. SO THE SHEET IS SINGLE-SIDED AND THE STRIPS BUTT. With nothing on the back there is no flip to register: 164 cards are 4 pages on 4 sheets. Strip N's bottom edge IS strip N+1's top edge and one hairline is drawn on it, so a single stroke of the blade separates both and the piece that comes off is a true CARD_H — 28.0 mm, which is what the design says and what the felt mat's start tick is drawn to. The cut before this left a gutter with the line down the middle of it: one stroke still, but every piece came off 31 mm with bleed at each end, and a 31 mm card against a 28 mm tick on the mat is a mismatch you can see. The vertical ticks have come INSIDE the strip with the gutter gone: 2 mm down from the strip's top edge and 2 mm up from its bottom, sitting exactly on the card boundary. The sheet is laid in 28 mm STRIPS, not a grid, because the cards are no longer one width; ONE TIN TO A PAGE, in tray order, and a page never mixes tins — pages() fills a page from one tin and stops, so each tin can go onto its own colour of card stock, and every page header names the one tin on it. What is in each tin is DERIVED from the two decks' own card tables — sheet 14's mirror of SENTENCE_BUILDER_CARDS in lib/montree/dark-phonics/writing-shelf-language.ts, which the build refuses to run on if it has drifted, and sheet 13's CARDS. Sort by the coloured rule into its tin, and stop there: the cards sit LOOSE. The grammar symbol is a TEACHING mark and not a sorting axis — nobody divides thirteen cards into seven compartments, and the symbol's job is to be seen and asked about. Only the 45-card free set is worth compartments, to keep it findable. THE TIN AND THE APP'S LEDGER STAY INDEPENDENT: none of the nineteen new words was added to WORD_CLASSES / SENTENCE_BANK in writing-shelf-language.ts, re-affirmed by the owner 2026-09-14.
items.cut: Cut along every grey line → 164 cards, 28 mm tall and 12.3–51.2 mm wide. The cards are NOT a grid: a 28 mm strip holds cards butted left to right until the next one will not fit, and the strips BUTT — one full-width hairline is a shared edge, with a triangle at each end, so one stroke of the blade frees the card above it and the card below it and every piece comes off a true 28 mm. The vertical between two cards is a TICK — the same grey hairline, 2 mm down from the strip's top edge and 2 mm up from its bottom, sitting exactly on the card boundary — because a full-height vertical would run through the middle of the cards in every other strip. Cut the strips off the sheet first, then cut each strip into cards on its ticks. 62 pink, 20 blue, 37 green and 45 uncoloured (35 reader words + 10 blanks). Every card is cut in its PRINTED form, so many carry a capital or a full stop, and a tin holds several cards of the same word — that is the point: the tin lays its whole tier out at once.

ONE TIN TO A PAGE, in tray order — pink (page 1), blue (page 2), green (page 3), then the free set (page 4) — so a sheet never mixes tins and each goes onto its own colour of stock. Sort by the COLOURED RULE into four tins: 62 pink, 20 blue, 37 green and 45 uncoloured for free composition. Many cards carry a capital (`The`, `A`, `Cat`) or a full stop (`sat.`, `mat.`, `asleep.`), and a tin holds several cards of the same word — by design, not a misprint: the tin is sized to lay ALL of its tier's sentences out at once. Then stop: a tier tin holds its cards LOOSE. The grammar symbol centred above the word on the front — black triangle noun, red circle verb, dark blue triangle adjective, light blue triangle article, green crescent preposition, purple triangle pronoun, pink bar conjunction — is a TEACHING mark, not a sorting axis. Only the 45-card free set is worth dividing into compartments, to keep it findable.

items.title: Story starter cards ×14 — 80 × 120 mm
items.note: The supplement that unsticks Tray 5. A child who can read every card in the tin can still sit in front of an empty sentence line, because inventing a sentence out of nothing is a bigger leap than reading one. He pulls a card, says what he sees, builds THAT out of the tin — and then turns the card over. The back carries the one decodable sentence the picture is of, so the card corrects him itself and no adult has to be standing there. Not tied to any one lesson: it is on the tray all year. Same card as sheets 02 and 03 — 80 × 120 mm printed, mounted on coloured backing card to 100 × 140 — because these are picked up and physically TURNED, which is what a flip card is for. THE SENTENCE IS LOWER CASE and set in Comic Neue — teacher review of the printed proofs, 2026-09-12. These are the literal words a four-year-old says when he looks at the picture (“hen in a pen”, not “Hen in a pen”); the capital and the full stop are his to add when he writes it. SHEET 13 IS NOW THE EXCEPTION AND IT IS DELIBERATE: from 2026-09-13 sheet 14's eighteen SENTENCES print as sentences, capital first and full stop baked into the last word card. These fourteen are phrases about a picture, not sentences, so the lower-case rule still holds here and must not be tidied to match sheet 14. Comic Neue is the free SIL-OFL face metrically similar to Comic Sans MS, which is Microsoft-licensed and cannot be embedded in a PDF the shelf ships; adult text in the margin is still Andika. THE CARD FRAME IS NEW, and it is the whole of the second round of proofs (2026-09-12): the 1.5 mm square-cornered rule printed as a thin line floating in a large white margin — “a line someone drew” — rather than as a designed card. It is now a ROUNDED DOUBLE FRAME, identical on sheets 13 and 14 and imported constant for constant so the two decks cannot drift: 2.6 mm of stroke with a 5 mm outer corner radius, its OUTER edge 4 mm off the cut line on all four sides so the bleed the blade works into is even the whole way round, and a 0.4 mm hairline of the same colour 2.2 mm inside it, cornered to match. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. EVERY ONE OF THE FOURTEEN IS FRAMED, on both faces, AND THE FRAME COLOUR IS THE READING TIER — sheet 14’s Montessori pink / blue / green, the three hexes imported from that sheet’s builder so they cannot drift. The deck used to be framed in a neutral warm charcoal with “hen in a pen” alone in pink, and a neutral says nothing: a child cannot sort the tray by it and a teacher cannot hand out a level with it. Each card is now read against the classroom’s own three-colour code on the words printed on its back. PINK (#D45B86) is every content word a pure three-letter CVC, one sound a letter, and it takes TEN of the fourteen: cat on a mat, pig in a wig, hen in a pen, dog on a log, fox in a box, bug on a rug, rat in a hat, nut in a hut, ant on a pan, cub in a tub — “ant” is filed with the three-letter short-vowel words, and so are “fox” and “box”, the x notwithstanding. BLUE (#2F5FA6) is four letters or more with no consonant blend, and it takes NONE: every card on this deck that leaves three-letter CVC behind leaves it for a blend. The tier is wired through the builder all the same, so a future blue card frames, paginates and labels itself with no other change. GREEN (#2F7D4F) is a consonant blend anywhere on the card, and it takes FOUR: frog in a bog (fr), bee on a tree (tr), duck in a truck (tr), sheep asleep (sl, over the sh digraph). ONE TIER TO A PRINTED PAGE. The deck is ordered pink then green and a page is filled from one tier only, then left short rather than topped up from the next — the teacher prints each tier onto matching coloured card stock, so a mixed page is a page he cannot use. Ten pink cards at four a page is three pink sheets of 4 + 4 + 2, the two blank slots on the third being correct and not a gap to plug; the four green cards fill the fourth sheet. Every page header names its tier on both the picture side and the sentence side. THE GROUND IS PAPER WHITE ON EVERY CARD (2026-09-13). “bee on a tree” is drawn on a scanned textured sheet whose grain runs 226–245 within one picture. This sheet used to white-point a ground by the MEDIAN of its border, which puts the middle of that grain at paper white and leaves the dark half of it below — so the card printed as a soft grey box with a visible edge, the one thing a picture card must not have. It now uses the same paper() as sheet 14, imported rather than copied: the white point is taken BELOW the grain, at the 5th percentile of the border band and floored so art touching the border cannot drag it down, and everything above it clips to paper. Two of the fourteen are white-pointed (pig-wig, bee-tree); the other twelve were already paper and are left completely alone. THE ART IS TRIMMED TO ITS OWN INK AND FILLS THE BOX. The source drawings carry whatever white margin the generator gave them, and on the proofs that margin printed as dead space round a small subject. The builder now measures each drawing’s ink at build time — the box holding all but 0.2 % of its ink WEIGHT at each edge, so soft pencil shading and a light wash are kept while the fading tip of a ground scribble is not — crops to it, gives back an even 2 % breathing margin and fits the result into the whole 60 × 100 mm content box, aspect preserved and centred ON THE INK, which is also what fixed drawings printing low in the card. Every card reaches the full 60 mm width; a wide composition is simply shorter. The source files are never written to. ONE EM FOR BOTH DECKS. The sentence size is no longer a per-card result: 10.90 mm of em, a 7.3 mm cap height — three times the cap height of a reading book — sets every sentence on sheets 13 and 14, and a sentence of three words or fewer sets on ONE line wherever it fits at that em. The old wrap took whatever size each sentence could reach, so “The cat sat.” and “The ant sat.” set large on one line while “The sun sat.” — the same eleven characters — broke to two and came out visibly smaller. A longer sentence takes the fewest lines that fit at that same em, so the deck steps down in line count and never in type size. Holding EVERY three-word sentence to one line without exception would peg the em to the longest of them, “The penguin spat.”, at 8.4 mm — a small line of type adrift in a large white card, too timid to be read at arm’s length by the child it is for, and a waste of the frame. Letting that one card wrap to “the penguin / spat” costs one card on one green sheet and buys 30 % bigger letterforms on every other card in both decks. Six of sheet 13’s fourteen and seven of sheet 14’s eighteen take two or three lines at this em; the rest set on one, and every one of them sets at the same size.

items.title: Illustrated sentence cards ×18 — pink, blue and green, 80 × 120 mm
items.note: The graded picture-then-words card for Tray 5. Sheet 12 gives the tray its tin of loose words; this sheet gives it eighteen pictures, each with its one sentence on the BACK. He meets the picture, says what he sees, builds that out of the tin — and then TURNS THE CARD OVER and reads the line, which corrects him without an adult standing there. The sentence used to sit under the picture on the same face; teacher review of the printed proofs (2026-09-12) sent that back, because a picture with its words beside it is a LABEL and the child reads the words and stops looking. FRONT = the picture and nothing else, BACK = the sentence and nothing else: the Montessori three-part card, and sheet 13's structure exactly. THREE TIERS, AND THE COLOUR IS THE DIFFICULTY OF THE WORDS — the Montessori Pink, Blue and Green reading series: pink is pure three-letter CVC (The cat sat. · A pig in a wig.), blue is four letters or more with no blend (The ant naps. · The cat digs.), green is consonant blends, one blend a card (st, sp, bl, cr, nd, mp). ONE CARD IS CARRIED, and it keeps its own colour (2026-09-13): “A fox in a box.” is pink WORK — fox and box are three-letter words, and sheet 13 prints that same pair pink — but it sits at the HEAD OF THE BLUE GROUP because the teacher wanted one already-known card at the start of the harder tray, for familiarity. It keeps its POSITION in blue and its PINK FRAME. A pink card at the head of the blue tray says “you already know this one”; painting it blue would claim a difficulty the words do not have and would put the same two words in two different colours across the two Tray 5 decks. The carry is recorded in the data — card(..., carriedFrom: 1) in writing-shelf-language.ts, which sets frameTier and a carried flag — so it is not “corrected” back. Since 2026-09-13 the deck is imposed ONE GROUP TO A SHEET, so the carried card lands on the FIRST BLUE SHEET (sheet 3) as the single pink-framed card among three blue-framed ones — the clearest form of the signal, and that sheet still prints onto blue card stock. Its header reads “blue”, which names the group on it. The card carries NO written difficulty label, exactly as a pink-series card has never had “pink series” printed on it: ONE EVEN COLOUR FRAME round the content, the same on both faces and the same width on all four sides, is the whole signal. The solid colour bar that used to run along the top of the card is gone — it was the top of the border, and on the proof it read, correctly, as a border thicker on one side than the others. Mount tier 1 on PINK card, tier 2 on BLUE and tier 3 on GREEN and the tray sorts itself. THE CARD FRAME IS NEW, and it is the whole of the second round of proofs (2026-09-12): the 1.5 mm square-cornered rule printed as a thin line floating in a large white margin — “a line someone drew” — rather than as a designed card. It is now a ROUNDED DOUBLE FRAME, identical on sheets 13 and 14 and imported constant for constant so the two decks cannot drift: 2.6 mm of stroke with a 5 mm outer corner radius, its OUTER edge 4 mm off the cut line on all four sides so the bleed the blade works into is even the whole way round, and a 0.4 mm hairline of the same colour 2.2 mm inside it, cornered to match. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. The frame colour is still the only tier signal: no bars, no labels, no dots. THE SENTENCE IS SET AS A SENTENCE (2026-09-13), capital on the first word and a full stop on the last, in Comic Neue. THE RULE THIS REVERSES was locked 2026-09-12 and read: “lowercase sentence starts, never capitals — these read as literal spoken phrases, not formal sentences.” It was reversed because these eighteen are the sentences the child copies into sheet 15's book and meets in every reader, so a card that never shows him a sentence cannot teach him one. THE FULL STOP IS BAKED INTO THE LAST WORD CARD of sheet 12's tin — the owner's explicit choice over a separate punctuation tile — so the sentence is complete the moment the last card lands, and a tier tin can hold two cards of the same word. build_14.display_words() is the single transform and every sheet that prints a sentence calls through it, so the rule can be reversed again in one edit. SHEET 13 IS THE EXCEPTION and stays lower case: its story starters are phrases about a picture, not sentences. Comic Neue is the free SIL-OFL face metrically similar to Comic Sans MS, which is Microsoft-licensed and cannot be embedded in a shipped PDF; adult text in the margin is still Andika. Same 80 × 120 card as sheets 02, 03 and 13, so it takes the same 100 mm stands, and the same SHORT-EDGE duplex registration. TIER 3 IS COMPLETE at six: mp — “The cat can jump.” — landed with its drawing on 2026-09-12. Fifteen of the eighteen pictures are REUSED art — the Dark Phonics picture books (the-sat’s flashcard tiles, the-sad, the-hot, the-nap, the-dig, the-spat), the satpin-v2 story starters, the satpin-v2 CVC set (w08-sand), and fox-box, which is the same drawing sheet 13 already prints; only green’s blob, crab and jump were drawn for it, and they live in phonics-images/satpin-v2/blends/. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_14_sentence_builder_cards.py; the eighteen cards are NOT listed twice — SENTENCE_BUILDER_CARDS in lib/montree/dark-phonics/writing-shelf-language.ts is the one source and the builder refuses to run if it has drifted from it. Sheet 12 has since grown sun, hot and digs, so every pink and blue sentence can now be BUILT out of the tin as well as read. Tier 3’s blend words (star, penguin, blob, crab, dad, sand, jump) are outside the tin by design — a blend is past where the tin stops — so the green cards are reading-and-copying work; see SENTENCE_BUILDER_GAPS. THE ART IS TRIMMED TO ITS OWN INK AND FILLS THE BOX. The source drawings carry whatever white margin the generator gave them, and on the proofs that margin printed as dead space round a small subject. The builder now measures each drawing’s ink at build time — the box holding all but 0.2 % of its ink WEIGHT at each edge, so soft pencil shading and a light wash are kept while the fading tip of a ground scribble is not — crops to it, gives back an even 2 % breathing margin and fits the result into the whole 60 × 100 mm content box, aspect preserved and centred ON THE INK, which is also what fixed drawings printing low in the card. Every card reaches the full 60 mm width; a wide composition is simply shorter. The source files are never written to. ONE EM FOR BOTH DECKS. The sentence size is no longer a per-card result: 10.90 mm of em, a 7.3 mm cap height — three times the cap height of a reading book — sets every sentence on sheets 13 and 14, and a sentence of three words or fewer sets on ONE line wherever it fits at that em. The old wrap took whatever size each sentence could reach, so “The cat sat.” and “The ant sat.” set large on one line while “The sun sat.” — the same eleven characters — broke to two and came out visibly smaller. A longer sentence takes the fewest lines that fit at that same em, so the deck steps down in line count and never in type size. Holding EVERY three-word sentence to one line without exception would peg the em to the longest of them, “The penguin spat.”, at 8.4 mm — a small line of type adrift in a large white card, too timid to be read at arm’s length by the child it is for, and a waste of the frame. Letting that one card wrap to “the penguin / spat” costs one card on one green sheet and buys 30 % bigger letterforms on every other card in both decks. Six of sheet 13’s fourteen and seven of sheet 14’s eighteen take two or three lines at this em; the rest set on one, and every one of them sets at the same size.

items.title: My Writing Book — A5 booklet, 18 work pages, one a card
items.note: THE STEP THE SHELF WAS MISSING, and what replaces sheet 05's blank strips on Tray 5. A loose ruled strip is silent: the child builds “The cat digs.”, picks up a strip, and nothing on it says which sentence he is writing, so the strip became handwriting practice and was thrown away afterwards. THIS BOOK IS HIS OWN — his name goes in the plate on the cover — and every one of sheet 14's eighteen cards has a page in it carrying THAT CARD'S PICTURE, so the work closes at both ends: draw a card → build it from the tin (sheet 12) → find that picture in MY book → write the sentence under it → check it against the card back. 24 A5 pages: cover with the bookplate, a tracker, 18 work pages, a words page and a finishing page. NOTHING IS PRINTED ON THE LINES — no sentence, no model, no word bank, no card number: the model is the line of word cards lying in front of him, and a model printed on the page would make the tiles ornamental and turn the work into copying. The rule is the school three-line rule ported from build_tracing.py — dotted headline, dashed midline, solid baseline, u = 6.6 mm — which is the x-height sheet 12's word cards are printed at, so a word out of the tin is exactly the size of the word he writes under it. THE TIER IS A COLOUR AND NOTHING ELSE: a small coloured tab on each page's fore-edge, high for pink, middle for blue, low for green, so the closed book shows three blocks down its edge and he opens at his own colour without reading a word. Colours are sheet 14's TIER_C, imported. The picture band is fixed at 85 mm on every work page whatever the rule count, so the book reads as one book and not as eighteen layouts. IT IS PRINTED, FOLDED AND STAPLED, NOT CUT: six A4 landscape sheets, duplex on the SHORT edge, nested with sheet 1 outermost, folded on the centre and stapled twice through the fold — build_booklets.py's imposition, folio, bookplate and print note, imported and not copied, so it is the same physical object as the readers on the same shelf. THE CHILD KEEPS IT: it goes home with him when all eighteen pages are written, and not before, which is why page 3 is a tracker and page 23 is a finishing page rather than a blank. The art is sheet 14's PREPARED art (.build/sentence-builder/<slug>.jpg), never the source PNGs, so the picture on the page and the picture on the card cannot drift; run sheet 14 first if .build/ is empty. 15-writing-book-reading.pdf is the same 24 pages in READING order, A5, for proofing on screen — do not print that one. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_15_writing_book.py. Sheets 01–11 and 13–14 are untouched.
items.cut: No cutting at all — this is the one sheet on the shelf with no cut line on it. Print the six A4 landscape sheets, NEST them (sheet 1 outermost, sheet 6 innermost), fold the nested stack once on the centre line — the two short black tick marks at the head and foot of sheet 1 mark it — and staple twice through the fold, about 40 mm either side of the middle. A long-arm stapler reaches; a normal one does not, so fold, open flat, staple from the outside into a block of card and close it. 24 A5 pages, 18 of them work pages.

items.title: Grammar work — 18 sentences with a box above every word, + 34 symbols
items.paper: A4 portrait — pages 1–2 plain 100 gsm paper, page 3 250 gsm card
items.note: THE BRIDGE FROM TRAY 5 TO TRAY 8. These are the SAME eighteen sentences the child has already built out of sheet 12's word cards and written into sheet 15's book. He knows them, so this sheet asks a second question about the very same words: not what does it say, which is answered, but what is each word DOING. He reads one sentence and lays a cut-out grammar symbol above each word. Nothing has to be rebuilt out of the tins first, which is what used to stand between a child and this work. THE PLACEHOLDER IS IDENTICAL OVER EVERY WORD: a dashed box, 12 x 10 mm, hairline, charcoal at a third opacity, the SAME box over `the` and over `penguin`. It must not be shaped like the symbol it waits for, or sized to it, or the sheet answers its own question; check() proves every box on the run is one single signature — geometry, dash, colour, alpha, line width — and that each word has exactly one. THERE IS NO TIER COLOUR ON THIS SHEET. Pink, blue and green say WHICH TIN; here the question is grammar, and a tier colour would be a loud answer to a question nobody asked. Everything that is not a grammar symbol is drawn in the free set's warm charcoal #4F4A44 — the word ink, the baselines, the dashed boxes. THE WORDS ARE SET AT THE CARD'S OWN SIZE AND SPACING: 6.6 mm x-height, 38.4161 pt of Comic Neue solved off the face's own OS/2.sxHeight, G = 7.0 mm of word space, each word standing on a 0.5 mm rule that runs its CARD width. So a line of this sheet is a row of card-shaped places, and a child who would rather build it than read it may lay his actual word cards straight down on the line and they will fit, word for word, to a tenth of a millimetre; check() proves that against the tin's own widths. PAGES 1–2 ARE WORKED ON, so they are PLAIN PAPER and they are NOT CUT and NOT LAMINATED — nine sentences a page, packed and filled to the bottom. They are the one thing on this shelf a child puts symbols down on, and a laminated sheet would be a display piece. Print more when they wear out. PAGE 3 IS ONE REUSABLE SET, not sixty-five one-use pieces: sixty-five would be a craft afternoon and a lost envelope, thirty-four is a set he keeps. Symbols at 10 mm base height — the WORKING size, the Tray 8 token's, not the card's 3.6 mm miniature — in the tin's own relative proportions and colours, each centred on its own 16 x 16 mm square so small fingers have something to pick up: noun 8, article 10, adjective 4, verb 6, preposition 4, pronoun 1, conjunction 1 = 34. Those counts are CHECKED, not asserted by hand: cut_need() adds up the two most demanding sentences for every class at once — the child lays two out side by side — and check() refuses to build if the set cannot cover it. Pronoun and conjunction are needed ZERO times by these eighteen sentences (no `it`, no `and`); their one piece each is there because the symbol set is the Tray 8 set, and a set with two classes missing teaches that there are five. THERE IS NO ANSWER KEY ANYWHERE ON THE SHEET, and it does not need one: the word cards in his tin already carry the same symbol in miniature, 3.6 mm, centred over the word on sheet 12's FRONT. A child who cannot place `in` goes to the tin, finds the card that says `in` and sees the green crescent on it. He checks HIMSELF, against a card he has held a hundred times. That is why nothing on this sheet may whisper the answer. NOTHING HERE IS A SECOND COPY: the point size, G, the ink measurement, the seven part-of-speech classes and the symbol drawing are all sheet 12's, imported. If a word is reclassed in the tin, this sheet changes with it in the same edit and cannot disagree; check_no_duplicate_map() reads this file's own source and refuses to build if anyone ever pastes a word-to-class table into it. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_17_grammar_work.py. Sheets 01–11 and 13–15 are untouched.
items.cut: Pages 1–2 are NOT CUT — they are the sheets the child works on. Page 3 only: laminate it, THEN cut along every grey line → 34 symbols, each centred on its own 16 x 16 mm square. The rows BUTT, one full-width hairline a shared edge with a triangle at each end, so one stroke of the blade frees the row above it and the row below it; every vertical is a TICK running 2 mm into the row at each end, because no two rows share their piece boundaries. Keep the one set in an envelope with the two sentence sheets.

Page 3 on 250 gsm card: LAMINATE it, THEN cut → 34 grammar symbols on 16 mm squares at working size. One set, in an envelope with the two sentence sheets, on Tray 8 behind the symbol key card.

items.title: Sentence mats ×6 — pink, blue and green, each tier guided then blank, six sentences a mat, A4 magnetic
items.note: THE MAT THAT COMES AFTER THE FELT ONE, and the shelf’s magnetic printable. SIX A4 LANDSCAPE PAGES onto A4 magnetic sheet — EVERY TIER TWICE, GUIDED THEN BLANK, in that order: pink guided, pink blank, blue guided, blue blank, green guided, green blank. THE PAIR IS THE CONTROL OF ERROR. On the GUIDED page the tier’s six sentences are PRINTED ON THE LINE in GREY — the set’s warm charcoal #4F4A44, not the tier colour — and each word is set at the x where a real card’s ink falls when the cards are butted from the start tick, so a laid word card covers its printed word exactly; the descenders are KNOCKED OUT OF THE RULE so the tails read whole. THE PRINTED WORDS ARE GREY AND NEVER BLACK: his cards are black on white, so a black guide under a black card is a second card, while grey stays a mark on the mat, and when the line is full the guide has gone under the cards and the sentence he built is the only black on the row. They are NOT in the tier colour — the rule under them already is, and setting the words in it made one colour mean both which tier this is and what to lay here. The BLANK page is the same mat with the words gone: same art, same tick, same rule in the same places. He matches onto the printed words first and graduates to the blank. Placement, knockouts and the rule-stub floor are IMPORTED from build_16, so the felt mat and the magnetic mat cannot disagree about where a word sits. THE SHEET MAY BE CUT INTO SIX, and this is a change of premise: it used to be the one printable here that was never cut, and that is no longer true of it. It now carries a cut guide at EVERY ROW BOUNDARY in cutmarks.py’s house standard — a 0.25 mm light-grey hairline, edge to edge, with a black triangle at each end sitting on the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin — so one straight pass of the blade separates two rows at once and six rows become six small magnetic sentence mats, one sentence each. HORIZONTAL CUTS ONLY: a row is one piece, picture and line together, and a vertical cut would saw it in half. Leave the page whole and it is still one whole-tier mat; the cut is offered, not required. IT IS STILL NEVER LAMINATED — a laminated magnet will not hold a magnetic card, which is the whole of what this sheet is for. NOTHING SITS ACROSS A CUT: the artwork is inset 2.0 mm from the row’s top and bottom, which is the clearance the 32 mm row already gave its 28 mm card band and the tightest clearance this mat has anywhere, and clearance() proves it on a raster of the real pages rather than on this paragraph. The adult caption sits in the bottom margin BELOW the last cut line, so the six row mats carry no adult writing at all and the caption goes with the trim. EACH ROW IS THE SENTENCE’S ARTWORK at the left in a 62 mm box, a start tick, then the ruled line. THE LINE IS ONE LENGTH — 208.8 mm on every row of every page, NOT sized to its sentence — so the SENTENCE sets its own width and the mat does not tell him how many words to expect before he has read the picture. A4 LANDSCAPE IS ARITHMETIC, NOT TASTE: the longest sentence, ‘The sad dad sat in the sand.’, measures 174.6 mm of real word cards through build_12’s own card geometry, and only the landscape line holds it. Sheet 19 is the portrait companion and it takes PINK ONLY for exactly that reason — see its own note. Six rows of 32.0 mm fill the 192 mm of usable height exactly. IT DOES NOT REPLACE SHEET 16’S FELT MATS AND THEY DO NOT REPLACE IT. The felt mat is the A1 classroom work rug — a 104 × 144 mm frame for every picture card, the tier’s words printed on the line, the GUIDED mat a child works before he can hold a sentence in his head — and it is MADE, not printed, which is why it is deliberately absent from this manifest and from every sheet and paper total. This is the small magnetic one for a board. Two objects for the same job, at two sizes and two moments; keep both. The tier colours are SB.TIER_C, sheet 14’s, imported and never re-declared — verify() reads them back out of the finished content streams. The art is sheet 14’s PREPARED art in .build/sentence-builder/, capped at 200 dpi so a small drawing prints SMALL rather than soft; run sheet 14 first if .build/ is empty. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_18_sentence_mats.py, which builds sheet 19 in the same run. Sheets 01–15 and 17 are untouched.
items.cut: CUT ACROSS ONLY, OR NOT AT ALL. This sheet used to be the one printable in the folder that was never cut; that is no longer true. It now carries a cut guide at EVERY ROW BOUNDARY — the house 0.25 mm light-grey hairline, edge to edge, with a black triangle at each end on the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin — so one stroke of the blade frees the row above it and the row below it. Cut them all and a page becomes SIX small magnetic sentence mats, one sentence each, the picture and its line staying together on one piece; leave the page alone and it is one whole-tier mat. HORIZONTAL CUTS ONLY — a vertical cut would saw a row in half. Six pages: pink guided, pink blank, blue guided, blue blank, green guided, green blank. NEVER LAMINATE IT — lamination kills the magnetic grip and adds thickness the board cannot hold. The adult caption sits below the last cut line, so it goes with the trim and no row mat carries adult writing.
items.howToPrint: Print 6 pages SINGLE-SIDED at 100%, A4 LANDSCAPE, onto A4 magnetic sheet — six sheets, each tier’s guided page first and its blank page straight after it. Do NOT laminate. You MAY cut it: across only, along the grey lines, for six row mats a page — or leave the page whole. Feed magnetic stock ONE SHEET AT A TIME through the straightest paper path the printer has (rear or manual feed, never a tight curl), and let each sheet lie flat until it is dry. Check the 100% on the first one before running the rest: lay a word card from the tin over its printed word on a guided page and the card should cover the word exactly and sit square inside the row.

items.title: Sentence mats, portrait ×4 — pink and blue, each guided then blank, six sentences on one A4 portrait magnetic page
items.note: THE SAME MATERIAL TURNED PORTRAIT, now carrying PINK AND BLUE. Four A4 PORTRAIT pages onto A4 magnetic sheet: pink GUIDED, pink BLANK, blue GUIDED, blue BLANK — the same control-of-error pair sheet 18 makes in landscape, one tier after the other. All six of a tier’s sentences sit on ONE page, one to a row, with the PICTURE AT THE LEFT OF THE ROW and the line to its RIGHT, rather than the picture above the line. Same art, same tin-measured word placement, same descender knockouts, same cut guides, same magnetic stock, same never-laminate. WHY GREEN IS STILL ABSENT, AND WHY THAT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A CHOICE. A4 portrait at an 8 mm margin leaves 194 mm of usable width, and once the picture column and the start tick have taken theirs the line is 105.8 mm — half the landscape mat’s 208.8. Every sentence is measured through build_12’s own card geometry, so which tiers can exist here is READ OFF THE TIN and not decided. PINK FITS: its longest run, ‘The ant is sad.’, is 89.9 mm, leaving 15.9 mm spare. BLUE FITS TOO: its longest, ‘A fox in a box.’, is 91.6 mm, leaving 14.2 mm spare, and needed nothing but the tier added — off the one line in the builder that names which tiers exist in portrait. GREEN CANNOT HAVE THIS FORMAT AT ALL: three of its six overrun the 105.8 mm line — ‘The sad dad sat in the sand.’ at 174.6 mm, ‘The cat can jump.’ at 111.8 mm and ‘The penguin spat.’ at 106.9 mm. No geometry on this sheet shortens a sentence, so green cannot be built in portrait unless those three sentences themselves change in writing-shelf-language.ts, and the build refuses — by name and by millimetre — until they do. WHAT PORTRAIT BUYS BACK. The line is shorter but THE ROW IS TALLER: 46.8 mm against landscape’s 32.0, so the artwork is half again as tall even though it now sits beside the line instead of above it, and the picture box widens from 62 to 80 mm. That is the trade, and it is the reason to reach for this one rather than sheet 18 for a child who is still reading the picture more than the line. CUT GUIDES AT EVERY ROW BOUNDARY, HORIZONTALS ONLY, exactly as sheet 18: six row mats a page, or leave the page whole. NEVER LAMINATED — a laminated magnet will not hold a magnetic card. The tier colour is SB.TIER_C, sheet 14’s, imported and never re-declared. The art is sheet 14’s PREPARED art in .build/sentence-builder/, capped at 200 dpi; run sheet 14 first if .build/ is empty. ONE BUILDER MAKES BOTH SHEETS — scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_18_sentence_mats.py — because the moment the two are separate files the tick drifts on one of them and nobody notices until it is printed. Sheet 16’s A1 felt mats are MADE, not printed, and are deliberately absent from this manifest and from every paper total; this sheet neither replaces them nor is replaced by them. Sheets 01–15, 17 and 18 are untouched by it.

A cut guide sits at every row boundary: the house 0.25 mm light-grey hairline, edge to edge, with a black triangle at each end on the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin. Cut them and a page becomes SIX small magnetic sentence mats, one sentence each, the picture and its line staying together on one piece; leave the page alone and it is one whole-tier mat. HORIZONTAL CUTS ONLY — a vertical cut would saw a row in half. Four pages: pink guided, pink blank, blue guided, blue blank. NEVER LAMINATE IT — lamination kills the magnetic grip and adds thickness the board cannot hold.

You MAY cut it: across only, along the grey lines, for six row mats a page — or leave the page whole. Feed magnetic stock ONE SHEET AT A TIME through the straightest paper path the printer has (rear or manual feed, never a tight curl), and let each sheet lie flat until it is dry. Check the 100% on the first guided page before running the rest: lay a word card from the matching tin over its printed word and it should cover the word exactly.

items.title: Empty sentence frames ×18 — grammar symbols only, no words printed, three levels, six frames a page
items.note: THE FRAME SUPPLIES THE GRAMMAR AND HE SUPPLIES THE WORDS. Sheets 18 and 19 give him EIGHTEEN FIXED SENTENCES — a picture, a line and, on the guided page, the very words to lay. This sheet is the step past them. NOT ONE WORD IS PRINTED ANYWHERE ON IT. A row is a run of Montessori grammar symbols over an empty line: the child READS THE SYMBOLS, goes to his word tins, and builds a sentence of that SHAPE out of any words he can read. Six frames to a page, three pages, three shapes. THE THREE LEVELS, ONE A PAGE: level 1 article · noun · verb (The cat sat.); level 2 article · adjective · noun · verb (The sad cat sat.); level 3 article · noun · verb · preposition · article · noun (The cat sat in the box.). LEVEL 3 IS PLACED THERE BY CURRICULAR CONVENTION, NOT BY EVIDENCE, and that is recorded rather than left to look like a finding: Brown's morpheme order has children producing `in` and `on` before `a` and `the`, so a prepositional phrase is not, in acquisition terms, harder than an adjective. Montessori and ordinary K-1 practice both teach the adjective first — it drops into a noun phrase he already has — and hold the prepositional phrase back, and that is the order followed here because it is the order of the symbols this shelf already introduces. SUBJECT–VERB–OBJECT (The cat has a hat.) IS A PARALLEL THIRD RUNG, NOT A FOURTH — the same step, one more noun phrase after the verb — and it is not built because this shelf's verbs are nearly all intransitive (sat, naps, digs, spat, jump), so there is nothing for an object slot to hold. When the readers bring transitive verbs it is one more tuple in the builder. THE ROW: A4 portrait at an 8 mm margin, a 194 mm measure, six rows of 43.0 mm — a 10 mm SYMBOL BAND, a 3 mm gap, a 28 mm CARD BAND, which is build_12's own card height, so a real card laid on the line fills the band exactly. THERE ARE NO SLOT BOXES: a ruled box is a promise that the card lands inside it, and `penguin.` at 53.6 mm against a 40 mm noun slot would break it, so what is drawn is a row of symbols in order and the cards butt along one line as they do everywhere else on this shelf. The line runs the full 194 mm on EVERY row whatever the level, for sheet 18's reason — a line cut to its sentence tells him how many words to expect before he has read the symbols. The symbols are sheet 12's, drawn through build_12's own function under one scale, so no grammar colour is re-typed here. THE FULL STOP COMES OFF THE PUNCTUATION DISH, NOT THE TIN: the eighteen fixed sentences carry a printed stop on their last word card, but a sentence the child composes here has no such card and the free-composition tin holds none — there is no `.` in it and there cannot be, because the stop belongs to whichever word he happens to end on. So TRAY 5's DISH HOLDS THREE TILES AGAIN — stop, question mark, exclamation mark. Sheet 04 already prints all three, so nothing is reprinted; the stop tile goes back in the dish. Sheet 16's A1 felt mats are MADE, not printed, and stay absent from this manifest and from every paper total. Sheets 01–19 are untouched by this one.
items.cut: OPTIONAL, AND ACROSS ONLY. A cut guide sits at every row boundary — the house 0.25 mm light-grey hairline, edge to edge, with a black triangle at each end on the printer-safe margin. Cut them and a page becomes SIX SINGLE FRAMES, one shape each; leave the page alone and it is one sheet of six. HORIZONTAL CUTS ONLY — a vertical cut would saw a frame in half. The adult caption sits BELOW the last cut line, in the bottom margin, so it goes in the bin with the trim and the six frames carry no adult writing at all. NOT LAMINATED and not mounted — plain paper, printed again when it wears out.
items.howToPrint: Print 3 pages SINGLE-SIDED at 100%, A4 PORTRAIT, on plain 100–120 gsm paper — one level a page, in order. Do NOT laminate. You MAY cut it: across only, along the grey lines, for six single frames a page — or leave the page whole. Check the 100% before you run the rest: lay a word card from the tin on the line of any frame and its coloured rule should sit exactly on the printed line. Put the FULL-STOP TILE BACK IN THE DISH before this sheet goes on the tray — the child ends his own sentence with it, and no card here carries a stop.

items.title: Sentence frames with a drawing box ×18 — a 44 mm square he draws his subject in, then builds that sentence

items.note: THE FRAME WITH A SUBJECT, DRAWN. Sheet S gives him a row of grammar symbols over an empty line and asks him to build a sentence of that SHAPE out of his own word cards. It works, and it leaves him with nothing to build a sentence ABOUT. This is the same frame with a 44 mm SQUARE at the left of every row — the place the picture has held on sheets Q and R, so a child who has worked those mats reads the row the same way without being told. HE DRAWS HIS OWN SUBJECT in the square and then builds the sentence he has just drawn. STILL NOT ONE WORD IS PRINTED: the text layer of every page extracts to its one-line foot caption and nothing else, and the build refuses if it does not. The row grew from 43 to 46.33 mm to stand a 44 mm square, which is sheet R's portrait row arrived at from the other end; six frames still fit a page. The picture and a 3.5 mm gap take 47.5 of the 194 mm measure, so THE LINE IS 146 mm and sheet S's slot widths — the proportion of the tin's own card classes — are imported and multiplied by 146/194 and by nothing else, so level 3 still spans the line EXACTLY. The gap is 3.5 mm because of one sentence: level 3's own example, 'The cat sat in the box.', is 142.6 mm of real butted card, and at a wider gap it cleared the line by 1.4 mm, which is not clearance but luck. THE CAPTION IS ONE LINE, NOT SHEET S's TWO, and the square is why — six rows of 44 mm leave 11 mm of trim at the foot, and a second line would have to come out of the millimetre standing between the blade and a picture square. Sheet U is this same sheet with the square DASHED, for a picture tile to land on; all 114 fills of all three pages are identical between the two, read back off the finished files, and only the square differs. The full stop still comes off the punctuation dish: a sentence he composes has no full-stopped card and the free tin has none. items.note: THE FRAME WITH A SUBJECT, CHOSEN. The same sheet as T to the millimetre, with one difference: the 44 mm square at the left of every row is DASHED, in sheet P's own dashed-placeholder language — a third opacity, a 1.2/1.2 mm dash, the house hairline — because something lands on it. A 44 mm PICTURE TILE off sheet V lands there, and the child builds a sentence about the thing in the picture. THE RULE IS CENTRED ON THE 44 mm BOUNDARY so a laid tile covers half of it and leaves half showing: the dashed halo goes even all the way round when the tile is square on its landing, which is the control of placement. LAMINATE THIS ONE. Sheet T is paper and is drawn on once; this one is card, and it is worked again and again with the tiles. Everything else is T's: six frames a page, three levels one to a page, the 146 mm line, level 3 spanning it exactly, not one word printed anywhere, the one-line caption on the 11 mm foot, the cut lines across only. The two sheets are ONE MATERIAL IN TWO STATES and that is proved rather than asserted — every fill of every page is read back off both finished files and matched. items.title: Picture tiles ×40 — 44 mm, one object a tile, no word on any of them
items.cut: Every grey line, both ways — 5 down, and 7 across on sheet 1 and 5 on sheet 2 → 40 tiles of 44 × 44 mm, no blank cell anywhere
items.howToPrint: Print 2 pages single-sided at 100%, A4 portrait, onto 250 gsm card. LAMINATE FIRST, then cut along every grey line, down and across, for forty 44 mm tiles — sheet 1 gives 24 and sheet 2 gives 16, and the paper under sheet 2's last row is trim. They land on sheet U's dashed squares, so check the 100%: a cut tile must measure 44 mm on both sides.
items.note: THE BOX OF SUBJECTS. Sheet U prints a dashed 44 mm square and waits for something to land on it; this is the something. FORTY picture tiles, 44 mm square, ONE OBJECT A TILE — and NO WORD ON ANY OF THEM. A tile with 'cat' printed under the picture would hand him the noun card he is supposed to go and find, and the work would collapse into matching; the picture gives him the subject and the word is still his to fetch. The text layer of every page extracts to its foot caption and nothing else, and the build refuses if it does not. EVERY TILE IS A NOUN THE TIN HOLDS, checked against build_12's own word list and not against a second copy of it, because a picture of something he has no card for is a dead end. The tin grew on 2026-09-14 to cover sheets 13 AND 14 — 48 nouns — and this sheet grew with it, from 22 tiles to 40. WHOLE ROWS ONLY, AND NO BLANK CELL: four tiles fit across A4 and six down, so 40 is sheet 1 full and four rows of sheet 2, and the paper under the last row is trim rather than a blank card in the middle of a cut strip. THE EIGHT THE TIN HOLDS AND THIS SHEET DOES NOT PRINT ARE TWO DIFFERENT PROBLEMS, kept apart in the builder because the fix differs: 'cats' and 'moths' have NO ARTWORK ANYWHERE and need drawing; 'bog', 'cub', 'dad', 'hill', 'sand' and 'tip' HAVE artwork and are held back on style — bog's picture is a snowy forest path, cub's a bear in a field, dad's a lifestyle photograph, hill's and sand's landscapes, tip's a macro of a pen nib too abstract to name (its alternative carries a stock watermark). check() asserts that list is exactly the tin minus the tiles, so the build report cannot go stale. ONE SOURCE, ONE STYLE, WITH THREE NAMED EXCEPTIONS: 37 photographs come from docs/picture-bank/photos, whose house rule is a single object on a plain ground; 'cot' and 'rug' come from the satpin-v2 CVC studio set, which keeps the same rule; and 'blob' from the shelf's OWN blend artwork, because there is no photograph of a blob in the world and the black blob of 'The blob sat.' is the only blob this child has met. Nothing is taken from the sentence art, which draws a whole SENTENCE — the cat SITTING, the ant DIGGING — and a tile that already shows the verb has answered the question. THE TILE IS NEVER CROPPED TO SQUARE. That was measured first and thrown away: the crab's own ink is 1214 px across a frame 896 tall, the penguin's 1259, so a square crop would take a blade to a third of them. Instead the DEAD MARGIN is cropped and nothing else — the object's extent read off the picture's own ink, cut at the 0.3% of mass at each end so a soft vignette cannot drag the box to the frame edge — and the crop is contained in the tile's field at its own aspect. AND THE THRESHOLD IS READ OFF EACH PICTURE'S OWN GROUND rather than fixed: a flat studio white needs almost nothing, but the blob is drawn on a grainy sheet whose grain cleared a fixed floor everywhere, so every column carried mass and the blob came out printed at a fifth of its proper size. The floor is now the 99.5th percentile of the border ring's own wander plus a margin, and the crop is then CHECKED AGAINST ITS OWN EDGES — if more of the crop's border is object than the conservative crop's border is, the threshold cut into something and the tile falls back. At a 12% breathing margin not one of the forty falls back and every one comes in under a tenth of a percent of edge. CONTENT STOPS 4 mm INSIDE EVERY TILE EDGE, this set's own rule for a cut card, doing a second job here: the bank's grounds are not all the same white, and 4 mm of paper each side means no two grounds ever touch, so a cut sheet reads as pictures on cards and not as patchwork. Every tile is prepared at 400 dpi, capped at prepare time. One note for the record: the picture bank's live star.jpg is a STARFRUIT, and this sheet takes the bank's own replaced frame, a five-pointed star. The bank is not edited from here. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_23_picture_tiles.py.

items.title: Sentence strips ×32 — one strip is one whole sentence, the row of word cards fused into one piece
items.cut: Across at every row boundary — 9 rows a page of 28 mm — then down each row on its ticks → 32 strips, 76.4 to 179.6 mm long
items.howToPrint: Print 2 pages single-sided at 100%, A4 portrait, onto 250 gsm card. LAMINATE, then cut: one stroke across at every grey line gives nine 28 mm rows a page, and each row then cuts down on its short ticks into the one, two or three strips on it. Check the 100% before you cut the lot — a cut strip must be exactly as long as its sentence built out of the tin, and that length is the whole control of error.
items.note: THE SENTENCE HE MATCHES AGAINST, BEFORE HE BUILDS IT. The owner worked the sentence building in class and found the step the tray was missing: the child takes down the tin, he is asked to build ‘The cat sat.’, and he has nothing to build it AGAINST — the sentence exists only as a thing that was said to him. This is that thing, printed. A STRIP IS THE ROW OF WORD CARDS FUSED INTO ONE PIECE, and that is the whole of the design: 28.0 mm tall, sheet L's card height, and exactly as long as the SUM of sheet L's measured card widths for that sentence's words. ‘The cat sat.’ is 76.4 mm of card and it is a 76.4 mm strip. He lays the strip on the mat's line and builds the sentence out of the tin DIRECTLY UNDERNEATH it, word under word; when the last card lands, his row ends where the strip ends. THE CONTROL OF ERROR IS LENGTH and nothing on the sheet says so — a card too many and his row overhangs, one missing and it falls short, a wrong word and a column stops lining up. EVERY WORD SITS AT THE X ITS OWN CARD'S INK LANDS ON, build_16's butted-card run imported rather than re-derived, so ink to ink across a word boundary is G — 7.0 mm — on the strip exactly as it is between two butted cards. THE TIER COLOUR IS THE BASELINE RULE, sheet L's 0.5 mm rule at sheet L's 9 mm, drawn before the words so the descenders cross it, and it makes the same continuous coloured line the child's own butted cards make underneath. THE WORDS ARE BLACK, sheet L's ink and not sheets Q/R's grey: those guide words are a ghost he COVERS with his cards, and the strip is never covered — it is the sentence he is reading. No frame, no tint, no grammar symbol (the symbol is the card's, and a second copy floating above his own card would make the strip a thing to copy instead of a thing to match), and no word-boundary ticks — the printed spaces ARE the boundaries, which is what G was chosen for. THIRTY-TWO SENTENCES, EVERY ONE THE TIN IS BUILT TO MAKE: sheet M's fourteen story starters and sheet N's eighteen sentence cards, derived from build_12.sentences() and put through build_14.display_words(), the set's one transform, so ‘cat on a mat’ prints ‘Cat on a mat.’ and asks the tin for the very cards it holds. Not one sentence is typed in the builder. PACKED ACROSS AS WELL AS DOWN: a 28 mm row takes strips left to right, butted with no gutter, until the next will not fit, and the ORDER IS NEVER SHUFFLED to pack tighter — tray order, then deck order, and a row that cannot take the next strip is left short. That took the pink tier from two sheets to one and the whole run from four to two. CUT ONCE, with sheet L's departure: one full-width hairline on every row boundary frees the rows above and below it at one stroke, the left edge is one full-height cut for the whole sheet, and every vertical inside the block is sheet L's 2 mm TICK — shared between two strips inside a row, the trim at its end — because the rows break at different x and a full-height line would saw through the strips above and below. Laminated: it is matched against, again and again, and never written on. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_24_sentence_strips.py.
